In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuropathological changes in athletes who suffer repeated concussions, with particular attention to the development of CTe.
the need to understand the role of concussion in the pathogenesis of CTE and the role of CTE as a cause of progressive dementia in retired athletes.
the need for further studies into the relationship between concussions and CTD as well as the possible co-morbidities of other neurodegenerative diseases in athletes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence or absence of CTE is not a simple function of the number of concussions sustained.
CTE is likely to be present in a minority of individuals who have had repeated concussions and have developed neurocognitive decline.
the presence of multiple concussions is neither a sufficient nor a necessary condition for the development of CTe.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CTE is not a necessary consequence of repetitive head injuries, and other factors may play a role.
the link between repeated concussions in athletes and the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as CTE is still unclear.
there is a lack of evidence for the existence of CTE as a distinct clinical entity in athletes with multiple concussive events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CTE is not the only cause of dementia in retired athletes with a history of multiple concussions.

not all athletes who have a history of repeated concussive and/or sub-concussive head trauma and who present with progressive cognitive decline will develop CTE, but may present with other neurological disorders such as AD, ALS, and PD.
the presence of CTE in retired football players is rare and the diagnosis is difficult to make.
